title: Why You Don't Have To Be Cool To Build Rapport https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2014/09/13/why-you-dont-have-to-be-cool-to-build-rapport/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin dismantles the widespread assumption that teachers must be culturally 'cool'—fluent in youth slang and trends—to build strong rapport with students. He describes how this strategy can feel deceptively successful at first, drawing students in quickly, before eventually backfiring as students stop respecting the teacher as a leader and start treating them as a disappointing peer. He argues that genuine, influential rapport instead comes from consistent day-to-day pleasantness, authenticity, humor, and a willingness to see the best in students, combined with firm follow-through and clear boundaries. The article insists this approach works regardless of a teacher's age, experience level, or personal style, making the point that teachers don't need to change who they are to build trust. The piece ends with direct reassurance that any teacher, as they are, can build the rapport needed for a peaceful classroom.
points: Trying to be culturally 'cool' with students to build rapport may work briefly but reliably backfires as respect erodes.
When rapport is built on being a 'friend' rather than a leader, students react with shock and disrespect when held accountable.
Genuine rapport comes from consistent, day-after-day pleasantness and authenticity, not from mirroring youth culture or slang.
Trusting rapport pairs gentle kindness with firm, clearly defined, consistently enforced boundaries.
This approach to rapport-building works for any teacher regardless of age or experience—no personal reinvention required.
quotes: There is a common misconception that you must be “cool” in order to build rapport.

Although building rapport is critically important for effective classroom management, any teacher behavior that unnaturally seeks to mirror age-group norms—through language, mannerisms, and attitudes—will backfire.
That is, until the bottom falls out and misbehavior skyrockets.
So instead of looking up to you as a leader they admire, they’ll look over at you as a friend who disappoints them.
Building trusting rapport is a byproduct of your consistent, day-after-day pleasantness and willingness to see the best in your students.
It’s the staggering combination of your gentle kindness and rock-solid adherence to clearly defined boundaries that offer the keys to the kingdom.
